title: SQL Fundamentals
tagline: tables as grids — master reading before writing

placementQuiz.q: A table in a relational database is best described as:
options: A flat file with no structure
A grid of named columns and rows
A hierarchical tree of nested objects
A key-value store with no schema
placementQuiz.explain: Tables are 2D grids: columns have names and types; rows are records.
* means "all columns"; no WHERE means "all rows".

placementQuiz.q: In SQL, string literals are written with:
placementQuiz.explain: Standard SQL uses single quotes for strings. Double quotes are for identifiers.
LIMIT caps the result set size. Use with ORDER BY for predictable results.

placementQuiz.q: Which clause sorts the result rows?
placementQuiz.explain: ORDER BY sorts output rows ascending or descending.

blocks.md: **The first sentence you will be asked to write in any SQL screen:** "Show me every employee in the Finance department, highest paid first." Everything after this lesson — joins, aggregates, window functions — is that one sentence with more clauses.
**A table is a grid of named columns and numbered rows. Columns have types; rows are records. No hidden magic.**

Think of a spreadsheet: each sheet = a table. Columns (A, B, C...) have headers and types. Rows (1, 2, 3...) hold data. SQL lets you query this grid declaratively — you say *what* you want, not *how* to scan it.

items: Columns = vertical: fixed name, type, position
Rows = horizontal: each row = one entity (employee, order, etc.)
No inherent row order — use ORDER BY to sort
NULL = missing/unknown value, not zero or empty string

blocks.label: basic select
blocks.py-pandas:
# All columns
employees

# Specific columns
employees[['name', 'salary']]

# With alias
employees.rename(columns={'name': 'employee_name'})[['employee_name', 'salary']]

# Limit
employees.head(10)
blocks.py-sqlalchemy:
# All columns
session.query(Employee).all()

# Specific columns
session.query(Employee.name, Employee.salary).all()

# With alias
session.query(Employee.name.label('employee_name'), Employee.salary).all()

# Limit
session.query(Employee).limit(10).all()

options: Name and salary for every employee
Only name and salary for the first row
items.explain: Column list restricts output columns; no WHERE means all rows.

items.explain: SELECT without FROM is valid in PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server — it returns computed values, handy for testing functions. Oracle is the exception: it requires SELECT … FROM DUAL.

blocks.label: expressions & literals
blocks.py-pandas:
# String concat
employees['greeting'] = 'Hello, ' + employees['name']

# Arithmetic
employees['annual_salary'] = employees['salary'] * 12
blocks.py-sqlalchemy:
# String concat
session.query(('Hello, ' + Employee.name).label('greeting')).all()

# Arithmetic
session.query((Employee.salary * 12).label('annual_salary')).all()

items.q: In standard SQL (ANSI), string concatenation uses:
items.explain: || is the ANSI standard. MySQL uses CONCAT(); SQL Server uses +.

options: Error — can't multiply column by literal
Only works if salary is integer

blocks.label: equality & comparison
blocks.py-pandas:
# Exact match
employees[employees['dept_id'] == 3]

# Not equal
employees[employees['dept_id'] != 3]

# Range
employees[(employees['salary'] >= 50000) & (employees['salary'] <= 80000)]

# Greater/less
employees[employees['hire_date'] > '2023-01-01']
blocks.py-sqlalchemy:
# Exact match
session.query(Employee).filter(Employee.dept_id == 3).all()

# Not equal
session.query(Employee).filter(Employee.dept_id != 3).all()

# Range
session.query(Employee).filter(Employee.salary.between(50000, 80000)).all()

# Greater/less
session.query(Employee).filter(Employee.hire_date > '2023-01-01').all()

blocks.label: NULL handling
blocks.py-pandas:
# Find NULL
employees[employees['manager_id'].isna()]

# Find NOT NULL
employees[employees['manager_id'].notna()]

blocks.prompt: Three employees — emp 1 and emp 3 have manager_id NULL, emp 2 reports to 1. What does `SELECT * FROM employees WHERE manager_id = NULL` return?

options: The two rows with NULL manager_id
An error — NULL is not a value

reveal.md: **No rows at all.** `manager_id = NULL` is never true — NULL means unknown, and "unknown = unknown" is unknown, not true. WHERE keeps only TRUE rows, so every row is discarded. The working filter is `IS NULL`.

items.q: To find rows where manager_id is missing, use:
items.explain: NULL is not a value — it's the absence of value. Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.
BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends. Equivalent to col >= 10 AND col <= 20.

blocks.label: order by & limit
blocks.py-pandas:
# Sort ascending
employees.sort_values('salary')

# Sort descending
employees.sort_values('salary', ascending=False)

# Multi-column
employees.sort_values(['dept_id', 'salary'], ascending=[True, False])

# Top 5
employees.nlargest(5, 'salary')

# Pagination
employees.iloc[10:20]
blocks.py-sqlalchemy:
# Sort ascending
session.query(Employee).order_by(Employee.salary).all()

# Sort descending
session.query(Employee).order_by(Employee.salary.desc()).all()

# Multi-column
session.query(Employee).order_by(Employee.dept_id, Employee.salary.desc()).all()

# Top 5
session.query(Employee).order_by(Employee.salary.desc()).limit(5).all()

# Pagination
session.query(Employee).order_by(Employee.id).offset(10).limit(10).all()

items.q: ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 3 returns:
items.explain: DESC = descending (high to low). LIMIT 3 takes first 3 after sort.

items.q: To get page 3 with 20 rows per page (0-indexed):
items.explain: Page 3 (0-indexed) means 3 pages come before it: skip 3 × 20 = 60 rows. OFFSET 60 LIMIT 20.

blocks.title: B105 dry run — FROM → WHERE (BETWEEN) → ORDER BY

stages.label: FROM
stages.sql: SELECT first_name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY emp_id;
stages.note: Logical step 1 — **FROM** hands every later clause the full grid: all 21 employees, nothing filtered or sorted yet.

stages.label: WHERE
stages.sql: SELECT first_name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 75000 ORDER BY emp_id;
stages.note: **WHERE** keeps only rows inside the inclusive range — 6 of 21 employees survive (on hr_edge, 5).

stages.label: ORDER BY
stages.sql: SELECT first_name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 75000 ORDER BY salary;
stages.note: **ORDER BY** sorts the survivors cheapest first — the final shape B105 asks for. Each stage is a complete query showing the intermediate table.

items.title: Select All Employees
items.statement: Return all columns for all employees. Input: employees(emp_id, first_name, last_name, email, dept_id, manager_id, hire_date, salary, job_title, commission). Expected: every column, every row — row order does not matter.

exercise.prompt: Return all columns for all employees.

items.title: Select Name and Salary
items.statement: Return only the three name/salary columns — first_name, last_name, salary — for every employee. Expected: 3 columns, all 21 rows (hr), any order.
hints: List columns after SELECT separated by commas.

exercise.prompt: Return first_name, last_name and salary for all employees.
exercise.solution: SELECT first_name, last_name, salary FROM employees;

items.title: Top 10 Highest Paid
items.statement: Find the 10 employees with the highest salary. Input: employees(...). Expected: all employee columns, highest salary first, at most 10 rows. Trap: two employees tie at 95000 exactly at the cut — a bare ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 10 can drop either one arbitrarily, so pin the order with a unique tie-breaker.
hints: Tie at the cut? Add a unique second key: ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id LIMIT 10

approaches.name: Brute
approaches.idea: Sort by salary descending and cut after 10 rows — fine until employees tie at the boundary.

code.code:
SELECT *
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 10;

approaches.cost: one sort of 21 rows, trivial at this size — but the 10th slot is arbitrary when two salaries tie
approaches.pitfalls: With the 95000 tie in hr, either employee can be dropped, so the answer changes between runs and reports disagree.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Add emp_id as a deterministic tie-breaker so the same 10 rows always come back.

code.code:
SELECT *
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id
LIMIT 10;

approaches.cost: the same single sort — the extra key costs nothing and makes the result reproducible
approaches.pitfalls: The tie-breaker must be unique: emp_id works, name does not (two Priya Sharmas exist in hr).

followups.q: Where do NULL salaries land in ORDER BY salary DESC?
followups.a: PostgreSQL sorts NULLs first on DESC by default — the NULL-salary row would top a 'highest paid' list, which usually needs an explicit NULLS LAST.

followups.q: How do you page beyond the top 10?
followups.a: Add OFFSET: LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10 for page 2 — with the identical ORDER BY so pages never overlap or skip rows.

followups.q: Why not just sort in the application?
followups.a: The database sorts once and ships 10 rows; the app would download all 21 and re-sort — fine at 21 rows, wasteful at 21 million.

items.title: Salary Range 50k-75k
items.statement: Find employees whose salary is between 50000 and 75000, inclusive on both ends. Expected: all employee columns for the 6 survivors in hr, any order. The trace above is the dry run of the optimal approach.

approaches.name: Brute
approaches.idea: Spell the range as two comparisons joined by AND — explicit and portable.
approaches.cost: one scan with a two-sided predicate — identical plan to the optimal form
approaches.pitfalls: Easy to type < instead of <= on the upper bound and silently drop the 75000 boundary row.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: BETWEEN states the inclusive range in a single token — the contract is visible at a glance.
approaches.cost: the parser rewrites BETWEEN to the same >= AND <= pair — same cost, clearer intent
approaches.pitfalls: BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends; a half-open range still needs the two-comparison form.

exercise.prompt: Return all columns for employees with salary between 50000 and 75000, inclusive.
exercise.solution: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 75000;

followups.a: Yes, but remember it is inclusive at both ends — for a day boundary use ts >= '2024-01-01' AND ts < '2024-01-02' instead of BETWEEN, or you double-count midnight rows.
Yes — it compares with the column's collation, so BETWEEN 'A' AND 'C' matches names from A to C in dictionary order.

blocks.md: 13 sourced problems from HackerRank SQL · LeetCode SQL 50. Titles link to the platform. Generated from `content/problems.json` by `scripts/sync-problems.mjs` — do not hand-edit this section.

items.title: Select All
items.statement: Query the employees table and return every column for every row.
hints: Pattern: basic SELECT — list the columns (or *) and the table.

approaches.name: Brute
approaches.idea: SELECT * expands to all columns at plan time; fine for ad-hoc exploration, but it couples the query to the table shape.
approaches.cost: scans every row and returns every column; network and memory scale with table width
approaches.pitfalls: Breaks downstream code if a column is added or reordered; avoid in production views.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Name the columns explicitly so the contract is stable and only needed data is shipped.

code.code:
SELECT emp_id, first_name, last_name, email, dept_id, manager_id, hire_date, salary, job_title, commission
FROM employees;

approaches.cost: same scan, but a narrower projection; lets the planner use a covering index later
approaches.pitfalls: Must be updated when a new column is genuinely needed.

exercise.prompt: Return all columns for all employees.
exercise.solution: SELECT emp_id, first_name, last_name, email, dept_id, manager_id, hire_date, salary, job_title, commission FROM employees;

followups.q: Why is SELECT * discouraged in production?
followups.a: It hides the column contract: a later ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN silently changes result shape and can break parsers, ORMs and cached plans.

followups.q: Does SELECT * always read every column from disk?
followups.a: On a heap table yes; a covering index can satisfy a narrower projection without touching the heap, which is why explicit columns matter for performance.

items.complexity: Time O(n) rows scanned. Space O(n) for the result set.

items.title: Higher Than 75 Marks
items.statement: List the first names of employees whose salary is above 100000, ordered by the last three characters of their last name, then by emp_id.
hints: Pattern: filter with WHERE, then sort with ORDER BY.
Clause: WHERE salary > 100000; ORDER BY RIGHT(last_name, 3), emp_id.
Skeleton: SELECT first_name FROM employees WHERE salary > 100000 ORDER BY RIGHT(last_name, 3), emp_id;

approaches.name: Brute
approaches.idea: Sort by a substring extracted with SUBSTRING; portable across dialects that lack RIGHT().

code.code:
SELECT first_name
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 100000
ORDER BY SUBSTRING(last_name FROM LENGTH(last_name) - 2), emp_id;

approaches.cost: one substring per row during the sort; O(n log n) comparisons
approaches.pitfalls: Off-by-one in the start position returns the wrong suffix; verify on short names.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Use RIGHT() which states intent directly and lets the planner recognise the suffix.

code.code:
SELECT first_name
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 100000
ORDER BY RIGHT(last_name, 3), emp_id;

approaches.cost: same O(n log n) sort, clearer intent, fewer characters
approaches.pitfalls: RIGHT() is PostgreSQL/MySQL/SQL Server; Oracle uses SUBSTR(last_name, -3).

exercise.prompt: Return first_name for employees with salary > 100000, ordered by the last 3 letters of last_name then emp_id.
exercise.solution: SELECT first_name FROM employees WHERE salary > 100000 ORDER BY RIGHT(last_name, 3), emp_id;

followups.q: Why add emp_id as a tie-breaker?
followups.a: Two employees can share the same 3-letter suffix; without a tie-breaker the order is unspecified and results become non-deterministic across runs.

followups.q: Can an index speed up ORDER BY RIGHT(last_name, 3)?
followups.a: A plain index on last_name cannot, because the sort key is a function of the column; you would need a functional index on RIGHT(last_name, 3).

items.complexity: Time O(n log n) for the sort after an O(n) filter. Space O(n) for the sort.

revisionCard: SELECT column_list FROM table — * means all columns
WHERE filters rows: =, <>, <, >, BETWEEN, IS NULL
ORDER BY col [ASC|DESC] — sorts result; LIMIT n — caps rows
NULL ≠ 0 ≠ '' — use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL to test
String concat: ANSI ||, MySQL CONCAT(), Python +

glossary.def: Named collection of rows with same column structure.
Vertical slice of a table; has name, type, position.
Missing/unknown value; not equal to anything including itself.
Boolean expression in WHERE clause that filters rows.
Selecting a subset of columns (vertical filtering).
